units.title: Unit 45 — Personality and behaviour
learningObjectives: Describe personality and outward behaviour using precise combinations for friendliness, frankness, energy and hostility.
Distinguish compliments such as bubbly personality and sharp wit from critical judgements such as abrasive manner and open hostility.
Use natural collocations for appearance, confidence, resemblance and age-related behaviour.
Recognise the figurative meaning and register of expressions such as a gruff exterior and a stubborn streak.

items.example: The mentoring programme helps students identify personality traits that influence teamwork.
items.note: Personality traits are relatively consistent features of a person's character; the phrase is neutral and analytical.

items.example: Reliability and patience are personal characteristics valued by the care team.
items.note: Personal characteristics is a broad expression for qualities and patterns of behaviour.

items.example: The siblings rebuilt a troubled relationship after years of disagreement.
items.note: Troubled relationship describes an ongoing connection marked by conflict or difficulty.

items.example: Her thinly disguised dislike of the policy became obvious during the debate.
items.note: Thinly disguised means the negative feeling is only barely concealed, rather than openly admitted.

items.pt: não ser o ponto forte de alguém
items.example: Impromptu speaking is not Daniel's strong point, although his written work is excellent.
items.note: Strong point refers to an ability or quality someone does particularly well; the possessive changes with the person.

items.example: Despite her flexibility at work, she has a stubborn streak when making personal plans.
items.note: A streak is one noticeable part of a person's character, not their entire personality.

items.pt: uma aparência ou atitude exterior ríspida
items.example: Behind his gruff exterior, the caretaker was considerate and patient.
items.note: Gruff exterior contrasts an apparently harsh manner with qualities that may be different underneath.

items.example: Her sharp wit enlivened the panel discussion without embarrassing anyone.
items.note: Sharp wit refers to quick, intelligent humour, not physical sharpness.

items.example: Interrupting the guest repeatedly was downright rude.
items.note: Downright intensifies a negative judgement and sounds emphatic and critical.

items.example: Years of pent-up anger surfaced when the neighbours finally discussed the dispute.
items.note: Pent-up anger is strong anger that has accumulated without being expressed openly.

items.example: The new manager's forthright manner made expectations clear from the start.
items.note: Forthright describes speaking directly and honestly; it need not mean deliberately offensive.

items.example: The proposal met with open hostility from several committee members.
items.note: Open hostility is undisguised antagonism, stronger than a merely cool response.

items.example: The interviewer avoided using intimidating characteristics as a measure of leadership.
items.note: Intimidating describes qualities or behaviour that make others feel nervous or threatened.

items.example: The two researchers developed a special relationship built on mutual respect.
items.note: A special relationship suggests an unusually close or valued connection, not necessarily a romantic one.

items.example: The volunteer seemed to have boundless energy throughout the weekend event.
items.note: Boundless strongly suggests seemingly unlimited energy; it is normally complimentary.

items.example: Constructive feedback can boost a trainee's confidence before an important presentation.
items.note: Boost confidence means raise how sure someone feels about their ability; it takes a possessive or named person.

items.example: The presenter has a bubbly personality that puts nervous guests at ease.
items.note: Bubbly personality is an approving, informal description of someone lively and cheerful.

items.example: The actor greeted the audience with a dazzling smile after the performance.
items.note: Dazzling smile is an expressive, highly complimentary description of an especially striking smile.

items.example: These two cousins bear a striking resemblance to each other despite growing up apart.
items.note: Bear a striking resemblance to means look remarkably similar; the verb agrees with the subject.

items.example: Her discretion and generosity are admirable qualities in a community leader.
items.note: Admirable qualities are character features that deserve praise or respect.

items.example: The photographer was surprised that the twins did not look their age.
items.note: Look your age means appear to be as old as you actually are; vary the possessive pronoun.

items.pt: agir de acordo com a própria idade
items.example: The coach told the adults to act their age after a childish argument.
items.note: Act your age concerns age-appropriate behaviour, and can sound disapproving or teasing.

items.example: The children were bursting with energy after their afternoon nap.
items.note: Bursting with energy is vivid and informal; it commonly suggests observable enthusiasm and activity.

items.pt: uma expressão facial vazia ou impassível
items.section: B · Other useful collocations for behaviour
items.example: His blank expression gave no clue about whether he understood the question.
items.note: Blank expression describes a face showing little emotion or comprehension.

items.section: B · Other useful collocations for behaviour
items.example: She offered a warm smile to each visitor entering the clinic.
items.note: A warm smile conveys kindness or friendliness; it is not about physical temperature.

items.section: B · Other useful collocations for behaviour
items.example: The revised timetable received a cool reception from the staff.
items.note: Cool reception is an unfriendly or unenthusiastic welcome; receive and give both combine naturally with it.

items.section: B · Other useful collocations for behaviour
items.example: The school issued a clear policy against unacceptable behaviour during exams.
items.note: Unacceptable behaviour is a firm evaluative phrase for conduct that breaches standards.

items.section: B · Other useful collocations for behaviour
items.example: Although the review sounded critical, the discussion afterwards was perfectly friendly.
items.note: Perfectly means entirely or quite here; it does not imply ideal behaviour in every respect.

items.pt: um jeito áspero e pouco amistoso
items.section: B · Other useful collocations for behaviour
items.example: An abrasive manner can undermine an otherwise useful suggestion.
items.note: Abrasive manner describes a harsh or tactless way of dealing with people.

items.example: The chair responded with thinly disguised contempt when the rules were ignored.
items.note: Contempt is a strong feeling of disrespect; thinly disguised signals that the feeling is barely hidden.

items.section: B · Other useful collocations for behaviour
items.example: Several spectators were found to be guilty of unacceptable behaviour at the venue.
items.note: Guilty of introduces responsibility for conduct, while unacceptable behaviour names what is criticised.

items.example: Careful listening and fairness are among her strongest points as a mediator.
items.note: Strong points refers to positive qualities or abilities; strongest points uses a superlative naturally.

units.title: Unit 46 — Space and time
learningObjectives: Describe physical space and housing conditions using conventional collocations and their interchangeable alternatives.
Distinguish valid space and room expressions from the fixed phrase a waste of space.
Use advanced expressions for historical change, memories, heritage and cultural achievements.
Choose time-related combinations such as within living memory, a bygone era and the foreseeable future accurately.

items.example: The storage cupboard was a confined space with barely enough room to turn around.
items.note: Confined space highlights physical restriction and may also be used in formal safety contexts.

items.example: The interns had to work in cramped conditions during the office renovation.
items.note: Cramped conditions means there is too little physical space for comfort or effective movement.

items.example: The design studio is short of space now that a second team has arrived.
items.note: Short of space means lacking enough usable area; short of room is also natural in many contexts.

items.example: We are short of room for another bookshelf in the hallway.
items.note: Short of room is a natural alternative to short of space when discussing capacity.

items.word: take up a lot of space
items.example: The old filing cabinets take up a lot of space beside the windows.
items.note: Take up space describes the physical area occupied by an object or activity.

items.word: take up a lot of room
items.example: A large dining table would take up a lot of room in that apartment.
items.note: Take up a lot of room is interchangeable with take up a lot of space in this context.

items.example: The hall has ample room for the entire audience and their luggage.
items.note: Ample room means more than enough space; the adjective has a positive, relatively formal tone.

items.example: The workshop provides ample space for small groups to work safely.
items.note: Ample space is an alternative to ample room when sufficient area is emphasised.

items.example: From the ridge, we could see a vast expanse of grassland stretching west.
items.note: Vast expanse describes an extensive, often open area such as land, sea or sky.

items.example: An unused staircase in the middle of the flat seemed a waste of space.
items.note: Waste of space is the conventional phrase; waste of room is not standard in this meaning.

items.example: The architect moved the doors to leave room for a wider corridor.
items.note: Leave room for means reserve sufficient space or capacity for something else.

items.example: Please leave space for the wheelchair beside the front row.
items.note: Leave space for is interchangeable with leave room for in many physical contexts.

items.example: There were several vacant parking spaces behind the community centre.
items.note: Vacant parking spaces means unoccupied places to park vehicles, not an unused car park building.

items.example: There is plenty of space along the back wall for another desk.
items.note: Plenty of space describes sufficient or generous available area in everyday English.

items.example: Over the course of time, the city's industrial buildings acquired new uses.
items.note: Over the course of time describes gradual change as time passes; it is more formal than over time.

items.example: Her research made a lasting contribution to the field of renewable energy.
items.note: Make a contribution to takes the preposition to; lasting stresses continuing importance.

items.example: The rescue operation will go down in history for its extraordinary coordination.
items.note: Go down in history means be remembered as historically significant, for better or worse.

items.example: The magazine ranked her among the most influential architects of all time.
items.note: Of all time strengthens a comparison by considering an entire historical period.

items.example: Many critics describe the early decades of radio as the golden era of broadcasting.
items.note: Golden era denotes a period widely regarded as especially successful; golden age is also natural.

items.example: The exhibition explores the golden age of scientific illustration.
items.note: Golden age is an established alternative to golden era for a period of notable achievement.

items.example: The smell of fresh bread can bring back memories of childhood holidays.
items.note: Bring back memories means evoke recollections; the subject can be a sound, place or smell.

items.example: The archive digitised the recordings to preserve them for posterity.
items.note: Preserve for posterity is relatively formal and means keep something for people in the future.

items.example: The railway carriage evokes the elegance of a bygone era.
items.note: Bygone era is slightly literary and points to a period that has passed, often long ago.

items.example: Volunteers hope to restore the neglected theatre to its former glory.
items.note: Restore to former glory means return something to a previously admired state, often its original beauty.

items.example: The bridge repairs should reach completion before winter.
items.note: Reach completion is a relatively formal way to describe a project being finished.

items.example: The first week of training is now a dim and distant memory for the whole team.
items.note: Dim and distant memory suggests a past event no longer remembered clearly.

items.example: Several decades have elapsed since the first version of the machine was built.
items.note: Elapsed is formal for time passing; it usually takes a measured period as subject.

items.pt: dentro da memória de pessoas ainda vivas
items.example: The town has experienced two major floods within living memory.
items.note: Within living memory means recent enough for people who are still alive to remember.

items.example: Decisions about education can shape our destiny over many years.
items.note: Shape our destiny uses shape figuratively to mean influence the course of future events.

items.example: Self-driving delivery vehicles may become commonplace in the not-so-distant future.
items.note: Not-so-distant future means relatively soon, but not necessarily immediately.

items.example: The research centre expects to keep its current opening hours for the foreseeable future.
items.note: Foreseeable future means the period ahead that can reasonably be anticipated or planned for.

items.example: A decade has elapsed since the school opened its new campus.
items.note: Has elapsed uses a measured span of time as its subject, meaning that the period has passed.

items.example: The foundation plans to restore a building that has stood empty for decades.
items.note: Restore a building means repair it to a former condition, often preserving historical features.
